keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. Cliopatria starts the kingdom in 450; the page's infobox has c. 480 and Teres 'exploiting the collapse of the Persian presence in Europe' after 480–479, while the Skudra page keeps the Persian governor at Doriscus until c. 465 and has Teres building up his kingdom 'in whose territory the Hebrus flowed' around 465. Drawn as the Hebrus valley only; the growth to Sitalces' extent is undated (ledger -450, confidence 1).

-450..-405, 105,364 km2 from the Struma and Iskar to the Black Sea and the Danube — Sitalces' realm as described ('from the Strymon and Iskar rivers in the west to the Black Sea and the Propontis in the east'; 'from Abdera in the south to the mouths of the Danube in the north'). The Greek coastal cities (Abdera, Maroneia, Byzantium, the Pontic colonies) are rightly left to the poleis; the infobox's 160,000 km2 is larger because it counts tributary tribes.

-404..-367. The co-rule of Seuthes II (405–391) and Amadocus I (410–390) and Cotys I's reunification (384) change rulers, not borders. The Thracian Chersonese is outside the shape, correctly: Cotys only took it 363–360 (ledger).

-366..-351. Covers Cotys I's gain and loss of the Chersonese (ledger -360/-357) and the partition of 360/357 among Cersobleptes (east of Tonzos and Hebrus), Amadocus II (Maroneia to the Maritsa) and Berisades/Cetriporis (Maroneia to the Strymon) — three co-heir kingdoms drawn as one state (rename event, not a split), since Cliopatria and the page treat them as the Odrysian kingdom.

-350..-338, 102,200 km2. The shape is right at its start but its span is not: Philip took the western kingdom in 347, the centre in 342 and the east in 341–340 ('Conquest by Philip II 340 BC'), two years before Cliopatria's end. New keyframes -347, -342, -340 and -325 below carry the shrinking kingdom; the ledger's losses do the same.

sources.title: Odrysian kingdom
sources.note: Infobox: foundation c. 480 BC, area 160,000 km2, conquest by Philip II 340, rebellion of Seuthes III c. 330, destruction of Seuthopolis c. 250, Sapaean conquest c. 30 BC. Teres founded it 'exploiting the collapse of the Persian presence in Europe due to failed invasion of Greece in 480–79'; Sitalces 'from the Strymon and Iskar rivers in the west to the Black Sea and the Propontis'; partition of 360/59 (Cersebleptes beyond the lower Hebros and Tonzos, Amadocus II between Maroneia and the Maritsa, Berisades from Maroneia to the Strymon); Heraion Teichos 351; garrisons expelled 347/346; campaign 342–340; inland Thrace 'put under the loose control of a Strategos'; Celts under Comontorius founded Tylis c. 278; king list.

sources.title: Teres I
sources.note: 'King of Thrace 460–445 BC' in the table (the Odrysian page has 480/450–430); 'united the 40 or more Thracian tribes under one banner'; daughter married to a Scythian ruler; 'died during a military campaign in 445 BC'; succeeded by Sitalces.

sources.title: Sitalces
sources.note: 'reigned 431–424 BC'; realm 'from Abdera in the south to the mouths of the Danube in the north' and 'from the Black Sea in the east to the sources of the Struma in the west'; alliance with Athens at the start of the Peloponnesian War; invaded Macedon in 429 'with a vast army that included 150,000 warriors'; 'killed in 424 by the Thracian Triballi'.

sources.title: Cotys I (Odrysian)
sources.note: King 384–360; Iphicrates married his daughter (390); Miltokythes took Sestos 363/362; 'By 360 BC, Cotys controlled almost all of the Chersonese peninsula'; murdered 360; Cersobleptes 'had to accept a partition of the kingdom with Amadocus II and Berisades'.

sources.title: Cersobleptes
sources.note: Inherited September 360; by 357 accepted Berisades and Amadocus as 'autonomous rulers of parts of Thrace', keeping the land 'east of the Tonzos and Hebrus rivers'; the Chersonese 'finally ceded to the Athenians in 357 BC'; defeated by Philip in 352, son hostage at Pella; 346 Athenian garrisons expelled; 342–340 campaign, 'By early 341 he had overrun the coast and taken Cabyle'; Cersobleptes and Teres III 'eliminated or subjugated'; Philippopolis and Cabyle founded.

sources.title: Philip II of Macedon
sources.note: 356 Crenides renamed Philippi; 'From 352 to 346 BC … reducing the Greek cities of the coast as far as the Hebrus'; 'In 347 BC, Philip advanced to the conquest of the eastern districts about Hebrus, and compelled the submission of the Thracian prince Cersobleptes'; 'In 342 BC, Philip led a military expedition north against the Scythians' and founded Philippopolis; sieges of Perinthus 340 and Byzantium 339 failed.

sources.title: Seuthes III
sources.note: 'securely attested between 324 and 312 BC'; revolted 'in about 325 BC, after Alexander's governor Zopyrion was killed'; 322: '8,000 cavalry and 20,000 infantry', 'fought each other to a draw' with Lysimachus; 313 backed Callatis' revolt and was defeated; 'acknowledged the overarching authority of Lysimachus'; residence at Seuthopolis 'perhaps around 320 BC'; 'ruled only part of Thrace' beside Spartocus of Cabyle; coins suggest he still ruled at Cassander's death (297).

sources.title: Seuthopolis
sources.note: Founded 'between 325–315 BC' by Seuthes III; 'the capital of the Odrysian kingdom'; under the Koprinka Reservoir near Kazanlak; 'In 281 BC it was sacked by Celts'.

sources.title: Tylis
sources.note: Celtic kingdom 'founded by Celts led by Comontorius in the 3rd century BC' after Lysimachia (277); at Tulovo, Stara Zagora Province, 42.5833N 25.55E; infobox 279–213; Cavarus' capital 'destroyed by the Thracians in 212 BC'.

sources.title: Lysimachus
sources.note: 'In 323 Lysimachus was assigned control of Thrace' as strategos; 'difficulties from the Thracian king Seuthes III'; suppressed the Black Sea cities' revolt (c. 315–313); founded Lysimachia 309; king 306/305; killed at Corupedium in (February) 281.

sources.title: Skudra
sources.note: Persian Thrace from 513; Odrysae submitted to Darius in 513; Persian rule in Macedon overthrown 479, Eion 475, Doriscus evacuated c. 465; 'Teres I, the king of the Odrysae tribe, in whose territory the Hebrus flowed' was building his kingdom around 465; the Odrysian kingdom listed as successor.

notes: Cliopatria's 'Odrysian Kingdom' (-450..-338, four near-identical shapes of about 105,000 km2) is the Odrysian kingdom of Thrace, which the page dates from c. 480 BC. One state: the tripartition of 360/357 (Cersobleptes, Amadocus II, Berisades/Cetriporis) and the Macedonian tributary period are recorded as rename and vassal events, not as separate states, because the page and Cliopatria treat the three co-heir kingdoms as one Odrysian kingdom. Changes against Cliopatria: the start moves from 450 to 480 (new keyframe, Hebrus valley only); the end moves from 338 to 281 — the independent kingdom fell to Philip in 340 (two years before Cliopatria's end), but the dynasty survived as a tributary and Seuthes III's revolt (c. 325) and Seuthopolis (c. 320–281) continue the state until the Celtic sack. The -350 shape is accepted only for -350..-348; new keyframes at -347, -342, -340 and -325 carry the shrinking realm. End date: Seuthopolis' own page has it 'sacked by Celts' in 281, the Odrysian page's infobox has 'Destruction of Seuthopolis c. 250' and discusses the 270s and the 250s (Antiochus II c. 252); 281 is used because the Celtic kingdom of Tylis replaced Seuthes' dynasty in the same valley c. 278. The Odrysian name persists on the page to Cotys IV (by 171–after 166) and the Sapaean kings (Cliopatria's 'Thracian Kingdom', -87..50, group eu-03) — a gap -280..-88 in which Cliopatria draws no Thracian polity; Tylis (c. 278–212) and the Getae of Dromichaetes need dossiers. Disagreements: Teres I 480/450–430 (Odrysian list) vs 460–445 (Teres I page) vs c. 465 (Skudra); Sitalces' invasion 429 (Sitalces page) vs 428 (Odrysian page); Cersobleptes' first defeat 352 (his page) vs 351 (Odrysian page); Cotys I's death 360 (his page and Cersobleptes') vs 359 (king list). The infobox area of 160,000 km2 exceeds Cliopatria's 105,000 km2 because the Greek coastal cities and the tributary tribes toward the Danube are not drawn. Counterparts without a dossier: 'Thracian tribes', 'Celts of Comontorius (Tylis)', 'Chalcidians', 'Perinthus and Byzantium', 'Callatis' are name strings; 'tylis' in successors is a slug for a state that needs a dossier. Gazetteer: Maritsa, Struma and Danube (rivers), Stara Zagora, Plovdiv, Edirne, Tekirdağ, Constanța, Macedonia (region) resolve; Kazanlak, Seuthopolis, Tylis/Tulovo, the Thracian Chersonese/Gallipoli, Abdera, Maroneia, Cabyle and the Haemus are given as coordinates or polygons. 'Chalcidice' is absent from the gazetteer and used anyway.
